text: MHHW (Mean Higher High Water) is the average height of the highest tide each day. Tides above it reach farther up shorelines, marshes and low-lying areas than usual.

NOAA projection: NOAA’s computer model of San Francisco Bay starts from the tide table and adds what it leaves out: storms, wind, air pressure, river flow and ocean conditions such as the higher sea levels of an El Niño winter. It runs about 2 days ahead and updates 4 times a day. It’s guidance, not an official forecast; follow National Weather Service advisories.

text: Here a “King Tide” is a day when the tide table at Monterey reaches the 1-year tide (provisional): a tide so high the ocean reaches it only about once a year on average. These come when the sun and moon line up, mostly in November, December and January. They’re worked out years ahead, so they don’t include storms, waves or ocean conditions. The colors show how high each day’s highest tide reaches at Monterey.

Around high tide, expect water higher up beaches and around coastal trails, creek mouths and harbors. Waves can reach farther than usual: stay off rocks and jetties and never turn your back on the ocean.

text: Here a “King Tide” is a day when the tide table reaches the 1-year tide at Redwood City: a tide so high the Bay reaches it only about once a year on average. These come when the sun and moon line up, mostly in November, December and January. They’re worked out years ahead, so it doesn’t include storms or ocean conditions: a King Tide on a calm day may only wet low paths, while a storm or an El Niño winter can push an ordinary high tide higher. These are places where the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission (BCDC) mapped water coming over the shoreline when the Bay is 1, 2 or 3 feet above an average high tide (MHHW). They are the low parts of the shoreline, not a list of every place that can flood.

Each spot’s level is turned into a tide height at NOAA’s Redwood City gauge: the average high tide there plus 1, 2 or 3 feet. The page compares that with the tide table, NOAA’s projection for the next 2 days, and after that the tide table plus how much higher than the tide table the Bay has been running.

The maps show still water: waves, wind and rain runoff can add more. They use ground heights from 2010–11, so newer levees or fill may not show. The average high tide differs a little around the Bay, so heights are approximate, mostly on the northern shoreline. Nothing here says a particular home or street will flood.

This past month the Bay has run about {off} ft higher than the tide table on average (over {days} days, at Redwood City). Spots marked “only if the Bay stays high” assume it keeps doing that; it isn’t a forecast.

text: If anyone is in danger, or water is coming into a home, call 911. This form doesn't send help.
shown_on: Report page, top (first sentence in bold)

text: Tell OneShoreline where you see flooding: water over a street or path, a creek or the Bay over its banks, or a road closed by water. Staff use reports to learn where and when flooding happens.

OneShoreline staff read every report. They may add it to the flood reports map with a short description and an approximate location (about a block). Your name, contact details and your own words are never shown on the map. A photo is shown only if staff choose to.
shown_on: Report page, "What happens to your report"

text: Staff review reports during working hours, so a report may take a day or more to appear on the map.
notes: Change once the storm review schedule is decided

text: Reports, including photos, are kept by OneShoreline and may be public records under the California Public Records Act. Leave out anything you don't want shared, such as faces, license plates or house numbers.
Don't walk or drive into floodwater to report it or take a photo.
Flood reporting isn't open yet. In an emergency, call 911.
